confidence_note: Chapters 3 and 5 read in an early-edition full text. The old 'Tracy asks himself every morning' opening was not found and is dropped; the 'one task makes the day a success' line is not stated in that form and is dropped.
facts: Chapter 3: the 80/20 rule, or Pareto Principle, named for Vilfredo Pareto who first wrote about it in 1895; Tracy applies it to tasks: about 20 percent of your tasks hold 80 percent of the value.
With ten items on a list, Tracy says two may be worth as much as the other eight together; often one item is worth more than the other nine combined. That item is the frog.
Tasks may take the same time, yet one or two contribute five or ten times the value of the others.
Most people procrastinate on the few valuable items and keep busy with the trivial many; they look busy all day yet accomplish little.
His rule: resist the temptation to clear up small things first. Before starting, ask whether the task is in the top 20 percent or the bottom 80.
Chapter 5, ABCDE: write the list for tomorrow ('think on paper') and put a letter before each item before starting the first one.
A is a must with serious consequences (visiting a key customer, a report the boss needs for a board meeting); several A tasks become A-1, A-2, A-3, and A-1 is the biggest, ugliest frog.
B should-do with mild consequences ('tadpoles'), e.g. returning an unimportant phone message or checking email; never do a B while an A is undone.
C is nice to do with no consequences (coffee or lunch with a coworker); D is delegate; E is eliminate, often kept out of habit or because you enjoy it.
Tracy says start A-1 immediately and stay with it until finished, and practise the method daily for a month.
scene_details: a list of ten items with one worth more than the other nine
a letter written in front of each item before the first task
an A-1 frog and a B tadpole
coffee with a coworker marked C
tension: A list of ten looks like ten equal jobs, yet Tracy says one of them outweighs the rest, and it is usually the one avoided.
opening_idea: Open on the ten-item list and the one item worth more than the other nine together.

lessons.idea: Rank by consequence before you start, so the hardest valuable task is not decided by mood.
lessons.anchor: A-1 versus the B tadpole: never do a B while an A is undone.
lessons.example: A shop owner sorting the day's calls by what happens if each is skipped.

reflect_final: Look at your list for tomorrow: which item would carry serious consequences if skipped, and which would nobody notice if it vanished?

use_cases.situation: Your list has twelve items and all feel urgent.
use_cases.move: Put a letter in front of each. Tracy says never do a B while an A is undone, so start with the A-1.

use_cases.situation: A teammate is always busy but the key report slips.
use_cases.move: Ask which item on their list is the A; suggest the coffee-and-inbox items wait until it is done.
Ask the group to mark each item D or E if someone else could do it or it could go, before assigning the rest.

pocket_idea: Before starting, put a letter on every item. Do no B until the A-1 is finished.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: On a ten-item list, Tracy says one item can outweigh the other nine put together, and that is the one people dodge.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Tracy tells you to letter your list: A for serious consequences, B for tadpoles, C for nice, D delegate, E eliminate; then do A-1 first.
